power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Self-Reported Precipitants of Psychosis, Mania, and Depression: An AI-Assisted Analysis of Reddit

text.text: We examined self-reported precipitants of mania, psychosis, and depression on Reddit using AIassisted code development and automated coding, with blinded human validation.
Analyses compared precipitants of mania (n = 337), psychosis (n = 339), and depression (n = 252).
Generic stress and sleep disruption were common to mania and psychosis but rare in depression.

Cannabis and trauma/abuse/assault were more frequently reported for psychosis, while antidepressants and positive activation/reward were more frequently reported for mania, and selfevaluative thought patterns and social isolation/rejection for depression.
Automated and human coding showed strong agreement (κ = 0.82), supporting the feasibility of AI-assisted analysis of perceived psychiatric precipitants.

Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia show substantial phenomenological, genetic, and neurobiological overlap, with evidence suggesting that they are more closely related etiologically to each other than either is to unipolar major depressive disorder [1, 2].
text.formatted: Bipolar disorder and schizophrenia show substantial phenomenological, genetic, and neurobiological overlap, with evidence suggesting that they are more closely related etiologically to each other than either is to unipolar major depressive disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: We therefore examined whether this overlap extends to self-reported precipitants of mania and psychosis.
We expected greater similarity between the precipitant profiles of mania and psychosis than between either state and depression.
Specifically, stress, sleep deprivation, and psychoactive substance use were expected to be reported more frequently as precipitants of mania and psychosis than of depression.

We further expected the valence of precipitating events to differentiate mania from psychosis, with positively valenced events more likely to be self-reported as precipitants of mania and negatively valenced events more likely to be self-reported as precipitants of psychosis.
These hypotheses are consistent with existing theoretical perspectives [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: These hypotheses are consistent with existing theoretical perspectives <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: An inductive, automated (ChatGPT) coding framework was developed and applied to relevant Reddit responses to reduce hypothesisdriven investigator influence, with subsequent validation by blinded human coding.

Reddit was searched platform-wide using ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol, OpenAI) with prespecified cause-, trigger-, and worsening-related queries for mania, psychosis, depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia.
The automated search was instructed to identify relevant threads meeting prespecified thread-level criteria.

Threads were eligible when the initiating post, including the thread title and the original poster's accompanying body text, directly asked respondents about their own causes, triggers, or worsening factors for the target condition.
Threads were excluded when the title appeared relevant but the accompanying original post text showed that the question concerned a different issue.

Twenty threads were retrieved and included; the authors did not manually select among retrieved eligible threads or supplement the corpus with additional threads identified after the initial search pass, thereby limiting investigator discretion in corpus composition.
Because retrieval was conducted in a finite automated search pass, however, additional eligible threads may not have been retrieved.
The unit of analysis was the user-bythread response-context, with multiple relevant comments from the same user within a thread combined.
The final dataset contained 1,138 responses.
Results presented here focus on mania (n = 337), psychosis (n = 339), and depression (n = 252).

Bipolar disorder (n = 69) and schizophrenia (n = 83) responses remained part of the dataset and code-development process but were excluded from the primary results and manual reliability check because of smaller sample sizes.
An additional 58 responses from a mixed schizophrenia/psychosis thread were retained in the dataset but excluded from code development and condition-specific analyses.
Although complete responses were retained for analysis, usernames and verbatim quotations are not reported to protect user privacy.
Precipitants were automatically extracted conservatively in near-verbatim form and pooled across conditions.

To reduce hypothesis-driven code development, condition labels were concealed while an automated, data-informed code set was iteratively consolidated through residual review and conceptual refinement, yielding 33 nonexclusive precipitant codes.
Responses could be coded for multiple precipitant codes, but each code was counted at most once per response; ambiguous precipitants were retained as residuals rather than forced into a code.

Automated-human coding agreement was assessed in a stratified random sample of 200 mania, psychosis, and depression responses manually recoded from the verbatim response text by investigator AB while blinded to the automated classifications.

Agreement was strong overall (97.6% overall agreement; Cohen's κ = 0.82; micro-averaged F1 = 0.83) and within each condition (mania: κ = 0.79, F1 = 0.81; psychosis: κ = 0.90, F1 = 0.90; depression: κ = 0.74, F1 = 0.76).

Review of coding disagreements indicated that disagreement was not synonymous with automated error: discrepancies sometimes favored automated coding, sometimes manual coding, and sometimes reflected defensible conceptual overlap or ambiguity between precipitant codes.
Generative AI assistance.

ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol, OpenAI) was used to assist with automated searching, screening, extraction, code development, coding, supplementary workbook preparation, and drafting and revising substantial portions of the manuscript.
The authors reviewed and edited the manuscript content and take responsibility for the final work.
Clear differences emerged in the precipitant profiles of mania, psychosis, and depression (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Clear differences emerged in the precipitant profiles of mania, psychosis, and depression (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Generic stress was reported at similar rates for mania (28.5%) and psychosis (26.5%), but much less often for depression (5.6%).
Sleep/circadian disruption showed a similar pattern, occurring in 29.4% of mania and 18.3% of psychosis responses compared with 2.0% of depression responses.
Mania was further characterized by major life transitions (18.7%), romantic events (16.3%), antidepressants (13.9%), and positive activation/excitement/reward (10.1%).
Psychosis was distinguished by mood/psychiatric states/symptoms (30.1%), cannabis (29.2%), trauma (20.4%), other psychoactive substances (13.0%), and psychedelics/entactogens (10.6%).
Depression showed a different profile, led by cognitive/self-evaluative precipitants (25.0%), family/interpersonal events (20.6%), and social isolation/rejection (20.2%).

Thus, mania and psychosis shared several broad precipitants, particularly generic stress and sleep disruption, while more specific event and substance codes differentiated the two states and depression showed a largely distinct pattern.
Fig. 1 Self-reported precipitants of mania, psychosis, and depression.
text.formatted: Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref> Self-reported precipitants of mania, psychosis, and depression.

text.text: Points indicate the percentage of responses in each condition that identified the corresponding precipitant.
Codes were nonexclusive; responses could be coded for multiple precipitant codes, but each code was counted at most once per response.
Results are generally consistent with existing empirical literature on risk factors associated with psychosis, mania, and depression.
Cannabis was the most commonly reported substance-related precipitant of psychosis in the current sample, and cannabis use is well established as a risk factor for psychosis [6].
text.formatted: Cannabis was the most commonly reported substance-related precipitant of psychosis in the current sample, and cannabis use is well established as a risk factor for psychosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Sleep/circadian disruption was the most frequently reported precipitant of mania, and prior research has identified shorter sleep as an antecedent of mania [7].
text.formatted: Sleep/circadian disruption was the most frequently reported precipitant of mania, and prior research has identified shorter sleep as an antecedent of mania <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: A paucity of references to generic stress as a precipitant of depression is noteworthy given the established role of stress in the onset and course of depression [8] but may partly reflect an attribution of causality to more specific adverse social circumstances (e.g., loneliness, isolation) or specific stressful life events (e.g., rejection/invalidation).
text.formatted: A paucity of references to generic stress as a precipitant of depression is noteworthy given the established role of stress in the onset and course of depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> but may partly reflect an attribution of causality to more specific adverse social circumstances (e.g., loneliness, isolation) or specific stressful life events (e.g., rejection/invalidation).

text.text: Responses also more frequently referenced self-evaluative thought patterns as precipitants of depression than of mania or psychosis.
In a broad sense, the precipitant profiles of psychosis and mania show greater similarity.
Generic stress, sleep/circadian disruption, and multiple substance-related precipitants were frequently reported for these states but rarely for depression.
It is noteworthy, however, that specific substance classes were more frequently reported as precipitants of psychosis (cannabis, psychedelics) and of mania (antidepressants [9]), respectively.
text.formatted: It is noteworthy, however, that specific substance classes were more frequently reported as precipitants of psychosis (cannabis, psychedelics) and of mania (antidepressants <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>), respectively.

text.text: The expectation that mania and psychosis might also be differentiated based on the valence of precipitating events is descriptively supported by the data.

For example, trauma/abuse/assault was more frequently reported as a precipitant of psychosis, whereas positive activation/excitement/reward was more frequently reported as a precipitant of mania, consistent with existing literature [10, 11].
text.formatted: For example, trauma/abuse/assault was more frequently reported as a precipitant of psychosis, whereas positive activation/excitement/reward was more frequently reported as a precipitant of mania, consistent with existing literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: Further differentiation of positive versus negative romantic events, life transitions, or work/academic/achievement events was not attempted because the near-verbatim coding procedure was designed to minimize contextual inference.
Automated code development and coding produced aggregate results broadly consistent with existing literature and showed strong agreement with blinded human coding.
Strong human-AI agreement has been reported for ChatGPT-assisted qualitative content analysis of online forum data [12].
text.formatted: Strong human-AI agreement has been reported for ChatGPT-assisted qualitative content analysis of online forum data <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Agreement was particularly high for explicit and relatively discrete codes, including sleep/circadian disruption, cannabis, antidepressants, and trauma/abuse/assault.

Agreement was lower for codes requiring greater contextual interpretation, such as societal/political/world precipitants, and for overlapping codes, such as interpersonal versus social isolation/rejection/invalidation precipitants.

Review of coding disagreements suggested few systematic problems specific to automated coding; disagreements frequently reflected genuinely ambiguous language, such as references to "COVID" that could plausibly denote physical illness, pandemic-related social disruption, or both.
Human-guided automated coding of unstructured self-report data may offer several advantages.

It can reduce hypothesis-driven investigator influence during code development, lessen the effects of human time and concentration constraints, and facilitate analysis of larger text corpora and replication of coding procedures.
The current findings are based on retrospective causal attributions by self-selected Reddit users and so may differ from associations identified through prospective designs or clinical assessments.
Threads were retrieved through a finite automated search rather than sampled exhaustively, and some codes overlapped conceptually.
The findings should therefore be interpreted as describing patterns in perceived precipitants rather than establishing causal relationships between precipitants and psychiatric states.
Ethics statement.
This study analyzed publicly available Reddit posts and comments and involved no interaction with users or access to nonpublic information.
Usernames were not analyzed or retained as study variables, and no attempt was made to identify or re-identify individual users.
Under University of Wisconsin-Madison guidance concerning analysis of publicly available data, prior IRB approval was not sought.
Funding.

This study received no external funding. Charles L. Raison has received research support from the Tiny Blue Dot Foundation, the Vail Health Foundation, and the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H), none of which supported the present study.

Verbatim Reddit responses and source links are not publicly shared because quoted text may permit reidentification of individual users through online search.
